entries.title: Spain: Hundreds of migrants attempt to swim toward Ceuta
entries.summary: Spain's Civil Guard, maritime Rescue Services and the Red Cross said they rescued migrants from the water. The interior minister acknowledged the country was facing an "extraordinary, exceptional situation."
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

Spain's Civil Guard, maritime Rescue Services and the Red Cross said they rescued migrants from the water. The interior minister acknowledged the country was facing an "extraordinary, exceptional situation."

Spanish authorities said on Wednesday that hundreds of migrants swam from Morocco attempting to reach the territory of Ceuta.

Border security was overwhelmed by the action, as it did not expect the surge.

What do we know about the migrant attempts to reach Ceuta?

"In the last few days, more than 1,500 migrants, including adults and minors, have reached Ceuta by sea,” the leader of Ceuta's government, Juan Jesus Vivas, told journalists.

"The reception centers are collapsed and saturated," he added.

Spain's Civil Guard, maritime Rescue Services and the Red Cross reportedly rescued some 117 migrants from the water.

Moroccan authorities also reportedly grabbed dozens from the water on their way to Spanish waters.

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told Spanish television channel laSexta that authorities were facing "an extraordinary, exceptional situation."

Grande-Marlaska added that "we are dealing with it with the means that we already have deployed there permanently."

He praised Moroccan authorities for their involvement, saying they were cooperating and that the relationship with the kingdom was "close and based on loyalty."

Mostly Moroccans seeking to swim across

The Spanish government did not confirm exactly how many migrants had reached the territory by swimming.

It also remains unclear why so many people sought to swim toward Spanish territory.

The swimmers were mostly Moroccans, along with a small number of Algerians who had been living in Morocco while trying to migrate to Europe, according to activists in Morocco and Ceuta.

The incident follows a Spanish Supreme Court ruling earlier this month which established that migrants arriving by sea cannot be immediately pushed back across the border without due process, unlike those crossing by land.

However, activists have discounted the probability that average Moroccans including those swimming toward Ceuta would be aware of such a ruling, dismissing a link between the ruling and the crossings.

Migrant arrivals in Spain through the Mediterranean enclaves Ceuta and Melilla, were lower this year compared to the same time last year, as many migrants have sought other routes like the Canary Islands.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Iran war: US launches strikes on Iran as 'powerful response'
entries.summary: The US military said the strikes were in response to Iranian strikes on US forces a day earlier. Trump had threatened to hit Iran "very hard" in response to its strikes. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran war: US launches strikes on Iran as 'powerful response'

Published July 30, 2026last updated July 30, 2026

The US military said the strikes were in response to Iranian strikes on US forces a day earlier. Trump had threatened to hit Iran "very hard" in response to its strikes. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The US military has announced striking Iran in 'powerful response' to attacks a day earlier
  • Donald Trump had said the US would hit Iran 'very hard'
  • Drone hits storage tanker at Egyptian port, security firm says

Read below for the latest developments concerning the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Thursday, July 30, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Iranian media report attacks around Qeshm island

Iranian media report attacks around Qeshm island

Three explosions were heard on Qeshm Island in Iran near the strategic Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency.

Tasnim said that a residential area on the island was hit.

There have also been reports of explosions in Abadan and Bushehr, two cities in the southwestern part of the country.

"At 04:00 am (0030 GMT) a point near Qeshm was attacked by the American enemy military," said Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of the southern Hormozgan province, according to the Mehr news agency.

"Points around Abadan city were attacked by missiles by the terrorist enemy of America," the Fars news agency reported, citing the deputy governor of Khuzestan.

Skip next section US launches new strikes against Iran

US launches new strikes against Iran

US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that US forces began launching strikes against Iran at 8 p.m. ET (0000 GMT). 

"The strikes are a powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East," the military wrote on X.

Earlier, President Donald Trump warned that the United States would hit Iran hard in retaliation for Iranian attacks on US forces in Jordan.

Skip next section READ: Iran signals gas price hike as fuel crisis looms

READ: Iran signals gas price hike as fuel crisis looms

Iran is moving closer to politically sensitive changes in gasoline pricing as the government struggles with a widening gap between domestic fuel production and consumption, exacerbated by the ongoing conflict with the US.

On July 25, government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said changes to fuel prices or rationing are "certain and unavoidable," although officials have yet to confirm whether the response will come through new quotas, higher prices or both.

Read more on how Iran, an oil powerhouse is short of gasoline.

Skip next section US-owned storage tanker hit by drone at Egyptian port — security firm

US-owned storage tanker hit by drone at Egyptian port — security firm

Ambrey, a British maritime security firm, released Wednesday an initial assessment stating that a drone had struck a US-owned gas storage tanker in the Egyptian port of Damietta.

An earlier statement from Egypt's Oil Ministry confirmed the fire at the port, but did not mention a drone attack. The ministry said the fire was dealt with immediately and there were no casualties.

It was not immediately clear who was responsible.

If confirmed, a strike by Iran or its allies would mark a significant escalation of the conflict.

US President Donald Trump said he had been briefed on the incident.

Skip next section Trump threatens to hit Iran 'very hard'

Trump threatens to hit Iran 'very hard'

US President Donald Trump said the United States would hit Iran very hard following an attack on US military personnel in Jordan.

"They’ve already apologized, but, you know, we got to smack them a little bit," he told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday.

"It’s our turn, and we’ll see if we get there with an agreement at some point. But we’re going to hit them very hard," Trump added.

The warning came after the lull in fighting appeared to end, quashing hopes of returning to negotiations.

On Wednesday, Saudi Arabia and the United States announced strikes on Iran-backed militants in Iraq, which Baghdad widely condemned. Saudi Arabia's direct involvement threatens to widen the already escalating conflict in the region.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the situation of Iran and wider Middle East.

As the conflict in the Middle East continues to escalate, US President Donald Trump vowed to retaliate against Iran for attacking US military personnel in Jordan.

Meanwhile, Ambrey, a British maritime security firm, reported that a drone strike hit a US-owned natural gas storage vessel at the Egyptian port of Damietta.

Stay tuned for more news and analysis. For our coverage of the conflict on Jul 29, 2026, you can catch our blog here.

entries.title: Explosions in Kyiv after Zelenskyy warns of Russian strikes
entries.summary: At least one person was killed in a Russian air strike on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Russia had "prepared a massive attack," citing air force reports.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Explosions in Kyiv after Zelenskyy warns of Russian strikes

July 30, 2026

At least one person was killed in a Russian air strike on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Russia had "prepared a massive attack," citing air force reports.

At least one person was killed in a Russian airstrike on Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine, the city's military administration said on Thursday.

Explosions were reported over the Ukrainian capital Kyiv in the early hours of Thursday, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia might conduct a "massive attack."

Both the Reuters and AFP news agency cited people on the ground as saying they heard explosions.

"Sadly, one death has been confirmed," the Kyiv city military administration wrote on Telegram in the early hours of Thursday.

Russia has struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles, said the city's mayor, Vitaly Klitschko, urging people to seek shelter. He added that a few non-residential sites in Kyiv caught fire.

"The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!" Klitschko said.

Meanwhile, the Polish Armed Forces announced on X that Poland had scrambled its fighter jets on Thursday to protect its airspace amid Russian air strikes on Ukraine.

"Fighter aircraft and an early warning aircraft have begun operations while ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance systems have reached a state of readiness," the post said, adding that the actions are of a preventive nature.

What did Zelenskyy say ahead of the Kyiv explosions?

The strikes come as Zelenskyy had warned of a "high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight."

"I received a report from Air Force Commander Anatolii Kryvonozhko. The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago," Zelenskyy said on X.

The Ukrainian president stressed that Ukrainians' safety depended on the willingness of Kyiv's allies to provide anti-missile defenses. His statements came on the heels of a trip to the US where he said President Donald Trump had agreed to give Ukraine licenses for Patriot missiles.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Report finds 2025 was deadliest year for antisemitic attacks outside Israel
entries.summary: Germany had the highest number of antisemitic incidents in 2025, both in absolute and relative terms, a report has found.
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

Germany had the highest number of antisemitic incidents in 2025, both in absolute and relative terms, a report has found.

A report released on Wednesday by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism group found a record rise in antisemitic attacks worldwide.

J7 looked at Jewish communities in Argentina, Australia, Canada, France, Germany, Britain and the United States, which together are home to more than 90% of Jewish people outside of Israel.

The report highlighted that some 20 people were murdered in antisemitic attacks in Australia, the UK and the US in 2025, in what was "the deadliest year for antisemitic attacks in the diaspora... since the AMIA attack in Buenos Aires in 1994," the report said.

The AMIA attack was a bombing that targeted a Jewish community center, leaving 85 people killed.

The deadliest event in 2025 was the mass shooting at a Hanukkah festival near Australia's Bondi Beach, where 15 people were killed.

"Antisemitism in our seven countries is no longer a surge; it is our new normal," the J7 task force said in a statement.

"Governments must stop reacting after Jews are attacked and start acting before, with real security funding, stronger laws and social media platforms that enforce their own rules," the statement said.

J7's report found more than 23,000 antisemitic incidents across the seven countries in 2025, a sharp rise from the 9,800 that were recorded in 2022.

Gaza war remains a factor

The report highlighted that anti-Zionism appeared to be a key motivating factor for the rise in antisemitism, accounting for 48% of incidents in Britain and 45% in the US.

According to the report, incidents increased in the years after the Gaza war, which was triggered after Hamas's deadly October 7 attack in 2023.

The report found a rise of 136% in antisemitic incidents from 2022 to 2025.

Although the total number of incidents fell from 2024 to 2025, the figure remains well above pre-October 7, 2023, levels, the report said.

Germany tops list of antisemitic attacks

While Australia topped the seven countries in terms of the sharp rise in antisemitic incidents, Germany stood out as the one with the highest number of antisemitic incidents, both in absolute and relative terms, the report found, nearly five times Australia's rate.



In 2025, there were nearly 70 incidents per 1,000 Jewish residents, with a total number of 8,725 cases up from 8,713 in 2024 and 2,610 in 2022

Right-wing extremism caused 807 of the total cases, up from 562 in 2024.

Meanwhile, the number of antisemitic attacks attributed to left-wing, anti-imperialist extremism also rose from 349 to 501 cases. Islamist extremist-linked incidents rose from 143 to 166.

The report found that "anti-Israel activism" accounted for 22.6% of all recorded incidents in Germany in 2025.

Josef Schuster, president of the German Central Council of Jews in Germany, said the numbers represented an "ongoing normalization of antisemitism" in Germany.

Schuster called on lawmakers "to close existing loopholes in criminal law and consistently criminalize calls for the destruction of the State of Israel."

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: How well are LGBTQ+ rights protected across Europe?
entries.summary: After the attack on Berlin’s Pride event on Saturday, the situation of the LGBTQ+ community in Germany is a topic of conversation. How well are queer rights protected in other European countries? An overview.
entries.content:
Europe

How well are LGBTQ+ rights protected across Europe?

July 29, 2026

After the attack on Berlin’s Pride event on Saturday, the situation of the LGBTQ+ community in Germany is a topic of conversation. How well are queer rights protected in other European countries? An overview.

Germany is still reeling from the weekend's car attack on its Berlin Pride celebration. Politicians are deep in discussion over which consequences the country should draw.

The center-left Social Democrats (SPD) are now mounting another effort to have LGBTQ+ rights enshrined in the German constitution, known as the Basic Law. Article 3 of the Basic Law addresses equality before the law, and currently states that, "no person shall be favored or disfavored because of sex, parentage, race, language, homeland and origin, faith or religious or political opinions. No person shall be disfavored because of disability." 

But no mention is made of gender identity or sexual orientation. The SPD wants to change that.

Germany: progressive, but with gaps

Germany still has areas in which queer people — that is, individuals who identify as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, intersex, asexual, non-binary, pangender and otherwise — are not yet fully equal under the law. In addition to the lack of constitutional protection, parentage law is a concern as well.

When a heterosexual couple has a child, the biological mother and her husband are automatically recognized as the child's legal parents. (When a heterosexual couple is unmarried, the biological father must submit a formal declaration to the youth welfare office to recognize his paternity to legally be considered the child's father.)

In queer family constellations, however, the legal situation is far more complex and often requires lengthy legal proceedings to establish parentage. Surrogacy, meanwhile, is illegal in German — a position the ruling conservative Christian Democratic (CDU) party has held for years. Despite having defended this position in the past, high-ranking CDU politician Jens Spahn recently disclosed he had sidestepped this ban and that he and his husband received a child via surrogacy in the US. He was pressured to resign from his position as parliamentary group leader as a result.

Hate crimes and violent attacks on queer people have increased, and many continue to report discrimination in their daily lives. But compared with other European nations, Germany still ranks relatively highly in terms of legal equality for queer people.

In a cross-comparison of 49 European countries, the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association (ILGA), a global umbrella organization for LGBTQ+ advocacy groups, ranks Germany seventh in terms of protection and equality for queer residents. Spain holds first place, while Russia comes in last place. 

Spain: a pioneer in Europe

Spain's pioneering role in LGBTQ+ rights is rooted in its recent history. Before the end of Francisco Franco's dictatorship in 1975, queer people in Spain were persecuted and imprisoned. The transformation that followed brought about a wave of liberalization and modernization.

The process of decriminalizing homosexuality began in 1979. In 2005, Spain opened marriage to same-sex couples, including full adoption rights. In 2023, the Spanish parliament passed a comprehensive self-determination law. Any person aged 16 or older can now change their legal gender and first name in official documents with a simple declaration at the civil registry office.

Transgender identities are no longer classified as disorders in Spain's healthcare system. Spain also has strong anti-discrimination laws, an independent equality authority, and a legal requirement for companies with more than 50 employees to implement active inclusion and diversity plans for LGBTQ+ staff.

According to regular surveys, these legal advances enjoy the support of a broad majority of Spain's population. Pride events such as Madrid Pride are among the largest in the world and receive support from government institutions across the political spectrum.

Other European countries with similarly progressive records include Malta, Iceland, Belgium and Denmark.

Italy: growing restrictions amid a shift to the right

Under the right-wing nationalist government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, pressure on the LGBTQ+ community has grown significantly in recent years.

Italy still does not have marriage equality, nor does it grant adoption rights to queer couples. The Interior Ministry and public prosecutors have even challenged previously issued birth certificates, resulting in some non-biological mothers being stripped of their legal motherhood years after their children were born.

In late 2024, Italy's parliament passed a law declaring surrogacy a "universal crime." As a result, citizens who have children through surrogacy abroad may face prison sentences and substantial fines upon their return.

Italy also lacks a national anti-discrimination law that explicitly criminalizes hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Arcigay, the country's largest LGBTQ+ organization, has recorded a worrying increase in violent offenses and hate crimes targeting queer people.

Hungary: Orban's legacy and its reversal?

Hungary's legal environment for LGBTQ+ people is also restrictive and has been shaped by years of systematic legislative tightening under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

In 2020, Hungary abolished the possibility for transgender people to amend the sex recorded in their birth register. Hungary's constitution explicitly defines marriage as a "union of one man and one woman." Same-sex couples are barred from adoption. In 2021, Hungary passed a law under the guise of "child protection" that prohibits any positive portrayal of homosexuality or transgender identities to minors. The law has since been ruled incompatible with EU law by the European Court of Justice.

However, Orban's successor, Peter Magyar, who took office in May 2026, may now be steering the country in a different direction. One indication for this was Budapest Pride in June 2026, which was a peaceful celebration attended by tens of thousands.

The event had been banned the year prior, with the government at the time citing assembly laws.

Magyar's government has also announced plans to fundamentally revise existing anti-LGBTQ+ legislation and bring it into line with EU law. But the queer community in Hungary remains cautious. Repealing Orban-era legislation is likely to be a complex undertaking that could face stiff political and social resistance.

Russia: systematic persecution

Russia has the most repressive anti-LGBTQ+ legislation in Europe according to the ILGA Rainbow Map. The Russian Supreme Court has designated what it called the "LGBT movement" as "extremist" and banned it — even though no such organization exists. Authorities continue carrying out raids targeting activists, publishers and private individuals. Prison sentences can go up to 12 years. Positive or neutral expressions of LGBTQ+ identities and lives is criminalized, and gender recognition procedures are banned. 

The Russian LGBTQ+ community has been under particular pressure since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which President Vladimir Putin has in the past argued is a proxy battle with the West and its attempts to undermine the "traditional family values" of Russian society by promoting LGBTQ+ rights.

Under the extremist designation, queer people in Russia, as well as relatives and supporting activists, often live in fear of police and state violence. Many have fled the country.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: France expels Russian media commentator over disinformation
entries.summary: Tensions between Xenia Fedorova and the French date back to 2017, when President Emmanuel Macron accused her of spreading "defamatory falsehoods."
entries.content:
France

France expels Russian media commentator over disinformation

July 29, 2026

Tensions between Xenia Fedorova and the French date back to 2017, when President Emmanuel Macron accused her of spreading "defamatory falsehoods."

Russian commentator Xenia Fedorova has been ordered to leave France, the country's Interior Ministry said Wednesday. She has been accused of disseminating Kremlin propaganda on French television and radio.

According to French newspaper Liberation, the expulsion order accuses Fedorova of acting "as a conduit for disinformation campaigns orchestrated by the Russian authorities" with the aim of "destabilising public order" in France.

According to the AFP news agency, Fedorova has been placed under house arrest since the order was issued.

Fedorova is the former chief of the Russia Today (RT) in France, which was ultimately banned in the country after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

She stayed in the country and became a commentator for broadcasting outlets owned by French billionaire Vincent Bollore's media conglomerate.

According to French daily Le Monde, Fedorova has been known to be a "protege" of Bollore.

Fedorova made frequent appearances on the CNews television channel and Europe 1 radio.

She also writes for Le Journal du Dimanche newspaper, where she has been accused of spreading Kremlin talking points about Ukraine and the West.

'Serious infringement' on free speech

Fedorova's employers reacted to her expulsion saying they were astonished, adding that the move amounted to "a particularly serious infringement of freedom of expression."

The media group said it would "provide their full support ‌to Ms. Fedorova during this decision."

The commentator's lawyer Emmanuel Piwnica told AFP that his client would "immediately" file an appeal against the order.

"Xenia Fedorova is a journalist," Piwnica told AFP, adding that she has "always carried out her work in the most proper manner possible."

Macron says Fedorova 'not a journalist'

Tensions between Fedorova and the French state go back as far as 2017, when President Emmanuel Macron criticized her and implied she was not a journalist.

"When media outlets spread defamatory falsehoods, they are no longer journalists. They are instruments of influence," Macron said.

In June, Macron was again asked to speak on the subject and he said his opinion had not changed.

Experts on disinformation had previously raised the alarm about the influence of figures like Fedorova in France, ahead of a presidential election next year.

Although there is no evidence of any links between Fedorova and the Kremlin, media advocates have said she should still be regarded as an agent of influence.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: K-pop's BTS opt out of new Asian music Grammy consideration
entries.summary: The K-pop sensation BTS, snubbed when nominated for Grammys in the past, say they're not interested in winning a new Asian music category.
entries.content:
South Korea

K-pop's BTS opt out of new Asian music Grammy consideration

July 29, 2026

The K-pop sensation BTS, snubbed when nominated for Grammys in the past, say they're not interested in winning a new Asian music category.

K-pop powerhouse BTS said on Wednesday that they would not submit songs for consideration for the 2027 Grammys next February. 

The seven band members issued the same Korean-language note online in concert.

What's the reason BTS doesn't want to be considered this year?

They said they did not want to be included in the new Grammy category, best Asian pop music performance, that's seen as a way to categorize releases across K-pop or J-pop and C-pop from Japan and China, respectively.

Newly reformed BTS, touring to promote a new album after returning from a military service hiatus, would seem to be among the frontrunners in the category. 

"We hope our music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language," the band's message read. "We thank Army [the band's colloquial term for the BTS fan base] and everyone who has always stood by us."

Critics of the new Grammy argued it could serve as an exclusionary barrier stopping Asian pop music from winning other awards. Proponents argued it was just the latest of numerous genres added to the list of more than 90 Grammy categories.

Has BTS won Grammys before?

No. But the band had been nominated for a total of five.

Three times they made the shortlist as the best pop duo or group performance, once they shared a nomination for best album of the year because of their contributions to Coldplay's "Music of Spheres," and also for their music video "Yet to Come."

Up until this year's ceremonies, no K-Pop act had ever won a Grammy Award.

"Golden" from the Netflix animated film "KPop Demon Hunters" won the best song for visual media, a decision that prompted elation in South Korea, despite the song's US roots and fictional performing artists.

BTS touring to promote 'ARIRANG' after military service return

BTS reformed and returned to frontline performance this year after a four-year hiatus. 

They have released and are now promoting a 14-track album, "ARIRANG" — named after Korea's most renowned traditional folk song and unofficial national anthem, roughly translating as "My Beloved One." 

The band has spent most of the summer in the Americas amid the World Cup and its world tour, including performing at the controversial halftime show of the World Cup final this month. 

This fifth studio album follows a four-year break as the band members completed South Korea's mandatory military service and pursued solo projects. 

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Iran war: Egypt's difficult balancing act
entries.summary: The US-Iran war has already had a negative economic impact on Egypt. Now new threats from the Houthi group in Yemen are likely to worsen that. At the same time, Egypt is trying to stay on good terms with all parties.
entries.content:
Egypt

US-Iran war: Egypt's difficult balancing act

July 29, 2026

The US-Iran war has already had a negative economic impact on Egypt. Now new threats from the Houthi group in Yemen are likely to worsen that. At the same time, Egypt is trying to stay on good terms with all parties.

The Suez Canal boasts an array of impressive statistics. At 193 kilometers (120 miles) long, the Egyptian waterway is located between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and it saves ships traveling between Europe and Asia approximately 10,700 kilometers. This is why, since it was opened in 1869, the canal has become one of the world's most important trade routes.

However unrest in the Middle East has seen shipping companies increasingly avoid the Suez Canal over the past couple of years. The Houthi rebel group in Yemen has targeted shipping in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, off the coast of Yemen. To get to the Suez Canal, ships must pass the Bab el-Mandeb and the Yemeni coast.

Recently the Houthis have again threatened to block ships passing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and there are fears that the trend to avoid the Suez Canal will accelerate. 

This is a huge problem for Egypt. Fees paid by shipping companies transiting the Suez Canal are an important source of revenue for the country.

According to Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, Egypt likely lost around $7 billion (€6.15 billion) from a decrease in traffic through the Suez Canal in 2024 alone. The Reuters news agency said that at times, losses could have been as much as $8 million (€7 million) in a month.

This is why the economic consequence of that loss extends well beyond shipping. Egypt has not been impacted by the Iran conflict in a major military way, but it is certainly seeing an economic effect.

Egypt loses billions on Suez Canal

"Economically, Egypt is in a very ambivalent situation," says Stefan Lukas, director of German think tank Middle East Minds.

During 2025 and 2026, revenues from canal transits actually went up again, mainly because oil from the Gulf states was transported via Saudi pipelines to the Red Sea and then onwards through the Suez Canal. This was to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, which is being blocked by Iran and the US in turns. But the new threats by the Houthis to block the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could interfere with this alternative route.

It's bad timing for Egypt: Rising energy prices and the International Monetary Fund's reforms are already putting tough limits on Cairo's financial flexibility.

"Higher energy prices have made imports more expensive and driven up inflation," says Hanna Voss, an expert on the region with Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation. "The uncertainty in the Red Sea and potential disruptions to the passage through Bab el-Mandeb are jeopardizing Suez Canal revenues."

Tourism into Egypt, capital inflows and the exchange rate for the Egyptian pound are sensitive to any changes. Additionally Egypt is heavily indebted and dependent on loans from the International Monetary Fund, or IMF, as well as investments and financial aid from the Gulf States.

Just how serious the situation already is, can be seen via other numbers. According to the Associated Press, Suez Canal revenues fell from $10.25 billion in 2023 to around $4 billion in 2024. During the same period, the number of ships passing through the waterway decreased from more than 26,000 to just over 13,000. Many shipping companies preferred to detour around Africa rather than risk Houthi attacks.

No short-term solution

As the US think tank Carnegie Middle East Center explains, Egypt cannot compensate for these losses on its own because of the country's current economic model. The government increasingly relies on large-scale state projects and military-controlled assets to generate growth, the think tank reports, while potentially productive investments and private growth are neglected. The result is growing dependence on foreign loans and investments.

In the short term at least, there are no new sources of revenue that could offset the decline in Suez revenues. Economic reforms, such as those required by the IMF, are also not progressing.

"Egypt has an interest in very rapid de-escalation," Voss states.

This is why Cairo supports mediation between the US and Iran, albeit less overtly than Qatar or Oman. The Egyptian government wants to secure its relationships with the US, Saudi Arabia and the UAE while simultaneously avoiding an open confrontation with Iran.

British think tank Chatham House describes Egypt's positioning as risk management. The goal is not to decide the regional power struggle but to minimize the economic damage to itself.

"The regime under al-Sissi is once again pursuing a two-pronged approach," Lukas from Middle East Minds explained.

Outwardly Egypt is demonstrating solidarity with Saudi Arabia, condemning the Houthis' threats and increasing security at the Suez Canal. But Egypt isn't openly opposing Iran and behind the scenes, is keeping communication channels with the Iranians open. That behavior is driven by Egypt's financial dependence on the wealthy Gulf states and the fear that the Suez Canal itself could become a target in the war, Lukas explained.

"All the neighboring states have an interest in stabilizing the regional order because they simply cannot afford a prolonged crisis," Voss added.

And that is precisely Egypt's dilemma. For Cairo, this isn't just about foreign policy. Every escalation in the Red Sea costs the country urgently needed foreign currency. Every move towards peace increases the chances of economic recovery.

"The crucial question is whether the [Houthis' threatened] blockade remains symbolic or takes effect," Lukas said.

In reality the Egyptian government has little influence on that or the course of the wider conflict. Any lasting peace or diplomacy won't be decided in Cairo but in Washington, Tehran and likely by the Houthi rebels themselves.

This story was originally published in German.

entries.title: German Muslims are alarmed by the Islamist terror attack in Berlin
entries.summary: Germany's Muslim organizations condemn the Islamist terrorist attack targeting Berlin's Pride celebrations and fear repercussions.
entries.content:
Germany

German Muslims are alarmed by Berlin Islamist terror attack

July 29, 2026

Germany's Muslim organizations condemn the Islamist terrorist attack targeting Berlin's Pride celebrations and fear repercussions.

The terrorist attack that struck Berlin's Pride celebration, or Christopher Street Day (CSD), late on Saturday evening has heightened fears and concerns about further Islamist attacks. Until Sunday evening, when security forces confronted 21-year-old Abdul B. and fatally shot him, most media outlets and the politicians responsible referred to a "suspected perpetrator" and "alleged motives".

Investigators are now relatively certain that the perpetrator was an Islamist, a radicalized Muslim with links to the "Islamic State" terror group. Politicians and security agencies are debating stricter laws and expanded surveillance powers. Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) is politically responsible for this area.

"With shock and profound dismay, we learned of yesterday's inhumane attack on the CSD," the Council of Berlin Imams stated across various channels just over twelve hours after the attack. The Council expressed its solidarity with the victims, their relatives, and the bereaved, and thanked the emergency responders. "This act, which we condemn in the strongest possible terms, demonstrates the terrible consequences to which hatred and hostility toward others can lead. Hatred leads to nothing good."

Two days later, once the perpetrator's Islamist background had been confirmed, the Council of Berlin Imams issued a second statement, this time in greater detail. It stated that the terrorist attack once again demonstrated that "religiously motivated extremism ... poses a real threat to our society."

"As imams, we cannot emphasize often enough that terror, hatred and violence have no religious legitimacy whatsoever. Anyone who uses the religion of Islam to commit violence against people because of their identity, their beliefs or their way of life, or even to kill them, is acting in direct contradiction to the ethical principles of our religion." The term "Islamism" does not appear anywhere in the 30-line statement.

The Council of Berlin Imams explicitly condemns "all violence against queer people and members of other minorities in our society". Such direct references to queer people are relatively uncommon in comparable statements.

The Council has repeatedly faced criticism. Some politicians of the ruling center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and several experts argue that it promotes views that are at odds with Germany's liberal democratic constitutional system. Others dispute that assessment.

The Council's latest statement suggests that the imams are keenly aware of the challenges involved. They note that "radicalization rarely happens overnight". More often, it is the result of a gradual process that unfolds online and across social media platforms. The priority, they argue, must be to reach young people at an early stage and "provide them with guidance, a sense of belonging and future prospects".

No single institution, they emphasize, can shoulder this responsibility alone.

A few months earlier, one imam had told DW that, for many young people, the internet had long since become the real mosque.

Islam is not the same as Islamism

"Some Muslims reject the term 'Islamism' because they fear that even the linguistic association with the word 'Islam' harms their religion," sociologist and religious education scholar Mouhanad Khorchide told DW.

The 54-year-old is the founding dean of the Centre for Islamic Theology at the University of Münster. He does not regard this concern as helpful: "If we categorically deny any connection between Islam and Islamism, we make the necessary substantive engagement with the issue all the more difficult."

After all, Khorchide argued, Islamists base their arguments on Islamic sources. They claim to speak in the name of Islam. In his view, it is therefore not enough simply to say that Islamist perpetrators have "nothing to do with Islam". What is needed instead is a nuanced engagement with the issue in order to "deprive Islamist ideologies of their credibility in the long term".

Berlin's Ahmadiyya community

The members of Berlin's Ahmadiyya Muslim community are devout Muslims belonging to a reform movement founded more than a century ago, whose teachings have led many Muslims to reject them as non-Islamic. As a result, they have also been persecuted by Islamists.

In the days following the attack, the Ahmadiyya mosque community in Berlin-Charlottenburg invited the public to a series of dialogue events scheduled for the coming days, as well as to an "open Friday prayer service on the topic of Islamism."

Burhan Kesici, chairman of the Islamic Council for the Federal Republic of Germany, condemned the attack "in the strongest possible terms" and expressed his sympathy. He concluded with the words: "Muslims in Germany stand for peace."

Central Council of Muslims in Germany: 'we condemn all forms of violence'

Similarly, the much longer statement issued by the Central Council of Muslims in Germany (KRM) describes the organization as "deeply shaken" by the attack. "As Muslim religious communities in Germany, we condemn all forms of violence, extremism, terrorism, and contempt for humanity in the strongest possible terms," it states. 

Like the Council of Berlin Imams, the Central Council of Muslims in Germany avoids using the term "queer", and states: "No one should become the target of violence because of their sexual orientation...". Addressing the perpetrator's "Islamist" motive, the Central Council describes the attack as yet another case "in which an extremist ideology misuses religious references to justify hatred and violence."

Islam and pluralism

According to Professor Khorchide of the University of Münster, many mosque communities, imams and Muslim organizations remain "stuck in an apologetic posture."

Their main concern, he says, is often "to defend Islam against sweeping accusations and to emphasize that violence and terrorism have nothing to do with Islam". Although this is "understandable in light of widespread anti-Muslim hostility", it does not go far enough, Khorchide said: "Anyone who wants to solve problems must first be willing to name them openly."

Khorchide also points to the conspicuous reluctance to mention the event itself, the "CSD," and the queer context in which it took place.

Some imams, he argues, avoid a "clear distancing from Islamism" because "on certain socio-political issues, such as attitudes toward sexual diversity or gender roles, they share conservative convictions, even though they naturally reject violence."

Precisely for that reason, he says, they must be willing to engage in self-critical reflection. "A credible Muslim voice is not one that relativizes problems," the academic says.

Eren Güvercin, deputy chairman of the relatively small Alhambra Society, is even more outspoken. Founded in 2017, the organization advocates a pluralistic Islam and has drawn criticism from established Muslim umbrella groups because of its broadly liberal orientation.

Güvercin speaks of a "deliberate decision" by many not to name "the motive behind the attack, namely Islamist hostility toward queer people," nor "the target of the attack, namely queer people and the CSD."

According to Güvercin, speaking openly about these issues would inevitably raise the question of what their own religious stance toward queer lives actually is, he told DW.

While people are generally able to clearly identify the motives behind far-right attacks, he argues that this willingness is completely absent when it comes to Islamist attacks. There is no serious or self-critical debate within Muslim communities about Islamism as an ideology, nor about hostility toward queer people or antisemitism, Güvercin says.

Muslim organizations that are unable to name problems openly will, in Güvercin's view, be unable to provide meaningful guidance. "Instead, young people find that guidance from Islamist influencers online."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: World Cup sell off: Has FIFA finally gone too far?
entries.summary: A new FIFA proposal to sell off a stake in the World Cup has been met with fury in the football world. Under Gianni Infantino’s presidency, FIFA has become increasingly profit-driven, but is this too much?
entries.content:
July 29, 2026

A new FIFA proposal to sell off a stake in the World Cup has been met with fury in the football world. Under Gianni Infantino’s presidency, FIFA has become increasingly profit-driven, but is this too much?

 "While you divide, we unite," Gianni Infantino wrote on social media on Monday, in a long missive aimed at his detractors. By Tuesday, he had united the football world — albeit in opposition to his latest scheme. 

Shortly after reports emerged in UK newspapers The Times and the Financial Times on Tuesday, FIFA confirmed its plans to create a new subsidiary, named FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). This would enable it to sell a minority stake in the World Cup's operations to private investors for billions of dollars.

Chief among FIFA's proposed investors is the investment vehicle, Thrive Eternal, headed by Joshua Kushner — younger brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.  

Why is FIFA's new World Cup plan controversial?

Other than the potential conflict of interest connection to Trump, with whom Infantino has grown close, there are significant concerns about transparency, corruption and whether FIFA has the remit to make such a move unilaterally.

"The World Cup is one of the few truly global sporting events, and that comes with a responsibility beyond maximizing revenue," Bret Myers, a professor of sports business practices at Villanova University in Pennsylvania, USA, told DW.

The US connection is important, with the model echoing the way that many US sports operate. Formula 1 too went through a similar process when it was bought by Liberty Media in 2017. Greg Maffei, a former Liberty CEO, has been a "key commercial adviser" to FIFA on the FFE plan.

"North American sports have long operated within a more commercial framework, where private ownership, franchise valuations, and investor involvement are widely accepted," Myers added.

"Football, particularly in Europe, has a much stronger tradition of clubs and competitions being viewed as cultural institutions rather than purely commercial assets."

More fundamentally, the concern is that this is the first step towards the World Cup, football's biggest prize, becoming privately owned.

"A minority investment is very different from relinquishing control," Myers said. However, it does represent a significant shift in how the World Cup is financed and managed commercially." 

World football's global governors are a nonprofit organization but sit on cash reserves of an estimated $8 billion (€7.02 billion) after a World Cup that saw ticket prices skyrocket.

Given FIFA's remit lies in developing football, rather than purely profiting from it, there is a sense that this is a move designed to shore up Infantino's power and, perhaps, encroach on the turf of the continental football federations he failed to include in the planning.

How do Infantino and FIFA aim to sell the plan?

FIFA has promised to invest profits back into the game, mostly by offering all 211 member associations a flat fee of $20 million in 2027, rising to $24 million by 2035. Associations must decide whether to accept those payments by September 19 or risk them being reduced or retracted.

"The president controls this huge pot of money and uses it to reward those that are loyal to him, that support him, and punish those that are not supportive of him," Miguel Maduro a former chairman of FIFA's Governance, Audit and Compliance Committee, told DW.

"FIFA could do lots of good things with money. But there is no system of checks and balances and accountability to make us sure that the money is actually going to be well spent by all national football associations. Everything that that's happened in the past makes me suspicious of how this money will end up being spent."

What has the reaction been from the footballing world?

Almost universally negative. National federations, world leaders and fan groups have all come out against the idea, with federations particularly peeved about the lack of consultation.

But perhaps the most surprising reaction came from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), who released a statement confirming it was "not consulted on the proposal and is disappointed" by the way in which it was released. Asia and Africa, are where Infantino's main power base lies, as together they have 101 of the 211 national associations — with each getting a vote on the president.

Similar misgivings were expressed by a number of powerful national football associations, including Germany's DFB.

"A line is being crossed here. There is a strong consensus among the member associations on this matter, as evidenced by several conversations I have had in recent days with Aleksander Ceferin [president of Europe's football governors UEFA] and other colleagues," said Hans-Joachim Watzke, a DFB vice president.

"If European football stands united in opposing these plans, it carries significant weight."

Who might oppose FIFA's World Cup plans?

UEFA seems in the best position to lead any revolt and has hit out at the plans, saying football is "not FIFA's to sell." It was a strongly worded statement of the type UEFA has released several times in recent months as its battle with FIFA plays out in public. Reports suggest UEFA will meet as soon as Wednesday to discuss their options.

Maduro backs UEFA's stance but said he'd like the current climate to serve as an opportunity for broader reform.

"I don't think UEFA has the same severity of problems that we find in FIFA, but I do think it also suffers from serious governance problems and that they need to be addressed," he said.

"Simply getting rid of Mr. Infantino but leaving the entire structure and model of governance of sports will be removing a couple of bad apples but leaving the tree that produced them in place."

How could this change football?

That the AFC and the CONCACAF (which governs North, Central America and Caribbean football) have criticized the way the latest plans were released, may have strengthened UEFA's hand in any thoughts of breakaway or boycott.

It may also lead to the continental federations uniting to find someone to oppose Infantino in next year's presidential election or in threats of boycotting next year's Women's World Cup.

But Maduro thinks such talk is often designed to appease the public before intentions are quietly shelved.

"What we've seen so far for the most part is that these statements, where they distance themselves from these kinds of initiatives of FIFA, are made under the pressure of public opinions. But then they actually never follow through."

Maduro went on to say that UEFA's increasingly strident opposition to FIFA is, at least in part, a reaction to an increased threat to its own highly lucrative Champions League. Should the proposed changes go through, Maduro expects World Cups to be more frequent and a further expansion of FIFA's recently expanded Club World Cup. 

"They will want to transform that into the big international football competition of clubs instead of the Champions League. That's what they will try to do because it will be in their commercial interest," he said.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold
